claim: The Ariño amber is from the Lower Cretaceous dinosaur bonebed of Ariño (Teruel, Spain).
source: Here, we describe the amber from the Lower Cretaceous dinosaur bonebed of Ariño (Teruel, Spain) using a multidisciplinary approach.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the geological age and location of the amber deposit.

claim: Amber is found in both a root layer with amber strictly in situ and a litter layer mainly composed of aerial pieces.
source: Amber is found in both a root layer with amber strictly in situ and a litter layer mainly composed of aerial pieces unusually rich in bioinclusions, encompassing 11 insect orders, arachnids, and a few plant and vertebrate remains, including a feather.
evidence: The manuscript describes the two distinct amber-bearing layers based on field observations and analysis.

claim: The Ariño amber bioinclusions encompass 11 insect orders, arachnids, and a few plant and vertebrate remains, including a feather.
source: Amber is found in both a root layer with amber strictly in situ and a litter layer mainly composed of aerial pieces unusually rich in bioinclusions, encompassing 11 insect orders, arachnids, and a few plant and vertebrate remains, including a feather.
evidence: The manuscript reports the diversity of bioinclusions found through examination of amber pieces.

claim: Ariño represents the most prolific and palaeobiologically diverse locality in which fossiliferous amber and a dinosaur bonebed have been found in association.
source: Ariño arguably represents the most prolific and palaeobiologically diverse locality in which fossiliferous amber and a dinosaur bonebed have been found in association, and the only one known where the vast majority of the palaeontological assemblage suffered no or low-grade pre-burial transport.
evidence: The manuscript compares Ariño to other known localities with both amber and dinosaur bonebeds, concluding its superiority in diversity and abundance.

claim: Ariño is the only known locality where the vast majority of the palaeontological assemblage suffered no or low-grade pre-burial transport.
source: Ariño arguably represents the most prolific and palaeobiologically diverse locality in which fossiliferous amber and a dinosaur bonebed have been found in association, and the only one known where the vast majority of the palaeontological assemblage suffered no or low-grade pre-burial transport.
evidence: The manuscript provides taphonomic analysis of the amber and fossil assemblages to support this claim.

claim: Fossiliferous amber associated with bonebeds including dinosaurs has been previously reported in only three occasions.
source: Although amber from the Cretaceous is often found together with other fossils such as plant and, more infrequently, vertebrate remains, fossiliferous amber associated with bonebeds including dinosaurs has been previously reported in only three occasions.
evidence: The manuscript reviews the literature on localities with both amber and dinosaur bonebeds.

claim: The Fouras/Bois Vert locality (Charente-Maritime, France) is lower Cenomanian in age (ca. 96–100.5 Ma).
source: Firstly, the lower Cenomanian (ca. 96–100.5 Ma) locality of Fouras/Bois Vert (Charente-Maritime, France) yielded diverse vertebrate remains, including about 50 dinosaur bone fragments, alongside plant macroremains, molluscs, and amber lumps, a few of which were fossiliferous (Néraudeau et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on the age of this locality.

claim: The Fouras/Bois Vert locality yielded about 50 dinosaur bone fragments.
source: Firstly, the lower Cenomanian (ca. 96–100.5 Ma) locality of Fouras/Bois Vert (Charente-Maritime, France) yielded diverse vertebrate remains, including about 50 dinosaur bone fragments, alongside plant macroremains, molluscs, and amber lumps, a few of which were fossiliferous (Néraudeau et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on the vertebrate remains from this locality.

claim: The Fouras/Bois Vert amber yielded ~110 bioinclusions belonging to arachnids, springtails and at least four insect orders.
source: From the latter, ~110 bioinclusions belonging to arachnids, springtails and, at least four insect orders have been reported, including several species described (Perrichot et al., 2007; Tihelka et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on bioinclusions from Fouras/Bois Vert amber.

claim: Amber is known from the upper Campanian (~73 Ma) Pipestone Creek bonebed (Alberta, Canada).
source: Secondly, amber is known from the upper Campanian (~73 Ma) Pipestone Creek bonebed (Alberta, Canada) (Tanke, 2004; Currie et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on the Pipestone Creek locality.

claim: More than 99% of the 3000 individual fossils recovered from Pipestone Creek belong to Pachyrhinosaurus.
source: Although >99% of the 3000 individual fossils recovered from this site belong to Pachyrhinosaurus, other dinosaurs, fish, turtles, lizards, and crocodilians were also found (Currie et al., 2008; Bell and Currie, 2016; Cockx et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on the vertebrate assemblage from Pipestone Creek.

claim: Six bioinclusions were recovered from ca. 50 cm3 of amber pieces from Pipestone Creek.
source: Six bioinclusions recovered from ca. 50 cm3 of typically <1 cm amber pieces were described (Cockx et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on bioinclusions from Pipestone Creek amber.

claim: Fossiliferous amber was found in Stratum 11 from the uppermost Maastrichtian (ca. 67–66 Ma) Bone Butte bonebed site (South Dakota, USA).
source: Lastly, fossiliferous amber was found in Stratum 11 from the uppermost Maastrichtian (ca. 67–66 Ma) Bone Butte bonebed site (South Dakota, USA) (DePalma, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on the Bone Butte locality.

claim: The Bone Butte site provided ~3000 mostly disarticulated fossils representing >50 species of dinosaurs and other vertebrates.
source: This site, belonging to the intensively studied Hell Creek Formation, provided ~3000 mostly disarticulated fossils representing >50 species of dinosaurs and other vertebrates; the non-vertebrate material included molluscs, ichnofossils, and plant macroremains, and was mostly found together with the fossiliferous amber (DePalma, 2010; DePalma et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on the fossil assemblage from Bone Butte.

claim: 22 bioinclusions were found in 400 g of collected amber from Bone Butte.
source: The palaeodiversity recovered from the latter, in contrast, was rather scarce, with 22 bioinclusions found in 400 g of collected amber (DePalma, 2010; DePalma et al., 2010; Nel et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on bioinclusions from Bone Butte amber.

claim: The Ariño deposit represents one of the most important Lower Cretaceous dinosaur sites from Europe.
source: The Ariño deposit represents one of the most important Lower Cretaceous dinosaur sites from Europe (Alcalá et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on the significance of the Ariño site.

claim: The Ariño outcrop is located within the Santa María open-pit coal mine (Ariño municipality, Teruel Province, Spain).
source: This outcrop, located within the Santa María open-pit coal mine (Ariño municipality, Teruel Province, Spain), takes part in the Oliete Sub-basin of the Maestrazgo Basin (eastern Iberian Peninsula) (Salas and Guimerà, 1996).
evidence: The manuscript provides the geographic location of the Ariño outcrop.

claim: The Escucha Formation is early Albian in age.
source: In this sub-basin, the siliciclastic Escucha Formation, early Albian in age (Peyrot et al., 2007; Bover-Arnal et al., 2016), was deposited overlying Aptian marine carbonates (Cervera et al., 1976).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on the age of the Escucha Formation.

claim: The Escucha Formation represents coastal environments that included barrier-island systems with back-barrier marshes and flood-tidal deltas.
source: This formation represents coastal environments that included barrier-island systems with back-barrier marshes and flood-tidal deltas (Rodríguez-López et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on the depositional environment of the Escucha Formation.

claim: The AR-1 level of the Ariño locality has ca. 600,000 m2 of surveyed surface.
source: The AR-1 level of the Ariño locality, with ca. 600,000 m2 of surveyed surface, consists of marls with a high concentration of organic matter occasionally forming coal, which underlie the lowest level of coal exploited in the Santa María mine (Figure 1, Video 1; Alcalá et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript provides data on the extent of the AR-1 level.

claim: The AR-1 level has yielded a rich and diverse vertebrate fossil record representing more than 10,000 fossils.
source: The AR-1 level has yielded a rich and diverse vertebrate fossil record representing more than 10,000 fossils namely found in more than 160 mono- or bitaxic concentrations of usually well-preserved, articulated or semi-articulated partial skeletons (Alcalá et al., 2012; Alcalá et al., 2018; Buscalioni et al., 2013; Villanueva-Amadoz et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on the vertebrate fossil record from AR-1.

claim: New species of freshwater and terrestrial turtles, crocodilians, and ornithischian dinosaurs have been described from Ariño.
source: From these, new species of freshwater and terrestrial turtles, crocodilians, and ornithischian dinosaurs–that is, the ornithopod Proa valdearinnoensis and the nodosaurid Europelta carbonensis– have been described (McDonald et al., 2012; Buscalioni et al., 2013; Kirkland et al., 2013; Pérez-García et al., 2015; Pérez-García et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on new species described from Ariño.

claim: The ornithopod Proa valdearinnoensis has been described from Ariño.
source: From these, new species of freshwater and terrestrial turtles, crocodilians, and ornithischian dinosaurs–that is, the ornithopod Proa valdearinnoensis and the nodosaurid Europelta carbonensis– have been described (McDonald et al., 2012; Buscalioni et al., 2013; Kirkland et al., 2013; Pérez-García et al., 2015; Pérez-García et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on the ornithopod species from Ariño.

claim: The nodosaurid Europelta carbonensis has been described from Ariño.
source: From these, new species of freshwater and terrestrial turtles, crocodilians, and ornithischian dinosaurs–that is, the ornithopod Proa valdearinnoensis and the nodosaurid Europelta carbonensis– have been described (McDonald et al., 2012; Buscalioni et al., 2013; Kirkland et al., 2013; Pérez-García et al., 2015; Pérez-García et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on the nodosaurid species from Ariño.

claim: Predatory dinosaurs were present in the Ariño ecosystem, as evidenced by coprolites, ichnites, and isolated allosauroidean teeth.
source: Predatory dinosaurs were also present in the Ariño ecosystem, as evidenced by coprolites, ichnites, and isolated allosauroidean teeth (Alcalá et al., 2012; Alcalá et al., 2018; Vajda et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on evidence for predatory dinosaurs at Ariño.

claim: Three ostracod species have been reported from Ariño.
source: Regarding the invertebrate record, three ostracod species (Tibert et al., 2013), as well as freshwater bivalves and gastropods, were reported (Alcalá et al., 2012; Kirkland et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on ostracods from Ariño.

claim: The Ariño palaeoenvironment was inferred as a freshwater swamp plain with perennial alkaline shallow lakes subjected to salinity fluctuations due to marine influence under a tropical–subtropical climate.
source: Based on the former geological and palaeontological data, the Ariño palaeoenvironment was inferred as a freshwater swamp plain with perennial alkaline shallow lakes subjected to salinity fluctuations due to marine influence under a tropical–subtropical climate (Alcalá et al., 2012; Tibert et al., 2013; Villanueva-Amadoz et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on the palaeoenvironmental reconstruction of Ariño.

claim: The level AR-1 was dated as early Albian (ca. 110 Ma) based on charophyte, palynological, and ostracod assemblages.
source: The level AR-1 was dated as early Albian (ca. 110 Ma) based on charophyte, palynological, and ostracod assemblages (Tibert et al., 2013; Villanueva-Amadoz et al., 2015; Vajda et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on the age determination of AR-1.

claim: The only previously described bioinclusion from Ariño amber was a tuft of three mammalian hair strands corresponding to the oldest hair reported in amber.
source: The only previously described bioinclusion from Ariño amber was a tuft of three remarkably well-preserved mammalian hair strands corresponding to the oldest hair reported in amber (Álvarez-Parra et al., 2020a).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous publication on a bioinclusion from Ariño amber.

claim: Two distinct amber-bearing layers are present in the Ariño AR-1 level.
source: Two distinct amber-bearing layers, a lower one and an upper one, are present in the Ariño AR-1 level (Figures 1 and 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes the two layers based on field observations and provides figures showing them.

claim: The lower layer overlies a level of carbonates of oligotrophic lacustrine origin showing the development of palaeosols at its top, including root marks.
source: The lower layer overlies a level of carbonates of oligotrophic lacustrine origin showing the development of palaeosols at its top, including root marks (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: The manuscript describes the stratigraphic relationship and provides figures showing the carbonates and root marks.

claim: The lower layer is characterised by abundant, irregular amber lumps 10–40 cm in length with protrusions, an opaque crust, an inner banding pattern, and lacking bioinclusions.
source: This layer is characterised by abundant, irregular amber lumps (i.e., kidney-shaped) 10–40 cm in length with protrusions, an opaque crust, an inner banding pattern, and lacking bioinclusions (Figure 2A, C and F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the characteristics of the lower layer amber based on observations and provides figures.

claim: The kidney-shaped amber pieces are distributed along the exposed area of the AR-1 level and, if not partially exposed due to weathering, are complete.
source: The kidney-shaped amber pieces are distributed along the exposed area of the AR-1 level and, if not partially exposed due to weathering, are complete.
evidence: The manuscript describes field observations of the distribution and preservation of kidney-shaped amber pieces.

claim: The opaque crust from the amber pieces has an irregular morphology and its ultrastructure shows delicate microprotrusions and no evidence of linear grooves.
source: The opaque crust from the amber pieces has an irregular morphology and its ultrastructure shows delicate microprotrusions and no evidence of linear grooves (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: The manuscript describes SEM observations of the amber surface and provides figures.

claim: The banding patterns are formed by variable densities of abundant bubble-like inclusions of different sizes, which are monophasic (solid), biphasic (solid+ liquid), or triphasic (solid+ liquid + gas).
source: The banding patterns are formed by variable densities of abundant bubble-like inclusions of different sizes, which are monophasic (solid), biphasic (solid+ liquid), or triphasic (solid+ liquid + gas) (Figure 2G).
evidence: The manuscript describes microscopic observations of the amber internal structure and provides a figure.

claim: Mineral crystals have been detected growing inwards within allegedly empty spaces left by larger bubble-like inclusions—these include pyrite cuboctahedrons and needle-shaped crystals from an iron sulphate mineral according to EDS analysis (likely szomolnokite, Fe2+SO4·H2O).
source: Mineral crystals have been detected growing inwards within allegedly empty spaces left by larger bubble-like inclusions—these include pyrite cuboctahedrons and needle-shaped crystals from an iron sulphate mineral according to EDS analysis (likely szomolnokite, Fe2+SO4·H2O) (Figure 2H,I, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The manuscript describes SEM-EDS analysis of mineral inclusions in amber and provides figures.

claim: The upper layer from the Ariño AR-1 level is rich in amber pieces of flow-, droplet-, and stalactite-shaped morphologies, which often show external and/or internal desiccation surfaces.
source: The upper layer from the Ariño AR-1 level is rich in amber pieces of flow-, droplet-, and stalactite-shaped morphologies, which often show external and/or internal desiccation surfaces (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations of the upper layer amber and provides figures.

claim: Small, almost spherical amber pieces about 1–5 cm in diameter, with an opaque crust similar to the kidney-shaped amber pieces, are present in the upper layer, yet rare.
source: Small, almost spherical amber pieces about 1–5 cm in diameter, with an opaque crust similar to the kidney-shaped amber pieces, are also present in this layer, yet rare; their surface is polished and more regular in patterning (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B-D).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations of a rare amber morphology in the upper layer and provides figures.

claim: The FTIR spectra of two stalactite-shaped amber pieces from Ariño are dominated by a small C-H stretching band at 2925 cm–1, an intense C-H band at 1457 cm–1, and an intense carbonyl band at 1707 cm–1.
source: The FTIR spectra of two stalactite-shaped amber pieces from Ariño are dominated by a small C-H stretching band at 2925 cm–1, an intense C-H band at 1457 cm–1, and an intense carbonyl band at 1707 cm–1 (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1, Figure 3—source data 2, Figure 3—source data 3), all characteristic of amber (Grimalt et al., 1988).
evidence: The manuscript reports FTIR spectroscopy results and provides a figure showing the spectra.

claim: The Ariño amber spectra are very similar to those from San Just amber, their main difference being the presence of a small band near 1200 cm-1 in the latter.
source: The Ariño amber spectra are very similar to those from San Just amber, their main difference being the presence of a small band near 1200 cm-1 in the latter.
evidence: The manuscript compares FTIR spectra from Ariño and San Just ambers.

claim: The composition of the organic solvent-extractable materials obtained by GC-MS, comprising the 32.5 % of the Ariño amber, is dominated by labdane resin acids and its diagenetic derivatives, with amberene (I; 1,6-dimethyl-5-isopentyltetralin) being the major component in the bulk extract.
source: On the other hand, the composition of the organic solvent-extractable materials obtained by GC-MS, comprising the 32.5 % of the Ariño amber, is dominated by labdane resin acids and its diagenetic derivatives, with amberene (I; 1,6-dimethyl-5-isopentyltetralin) being the major component in the bulk extract (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—source data 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports GC-MS analysis results and provides figures showing the chromatogram and chemical structures.

claim: The labdan-18-oic acids are dominant in the polar fraction of the organic extract from the amber.
source: The labdan-18-oic acids are dominant in the polar fraction of the organic extract from the amber.
evidence: The manuscript reports GC-MS analysis results of the polar fraction.

claim: The identification of the clerodane-family diterpene VI is noteworthy.
source: The identification of the clerodane-family diterpene VI is noteworthy.
evidence: The manuscript highlights a specific compound identified in the GC-MS analysis.

claim: The analyses show no evidence of significant terpenes of the pimarane/abietane family and discount the presence of ferruginol.
source: The analyses show no evidence of significant terpenes of the pimarane/abietane family and discount the presence of ferruginol.
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of certain compounds in the GC-MS analysis.

claim: The Ariño amber does not show a significant content of either 15-homoamberene (III) or 1-methylamberene (X).
source: The Ariño amber does not show a significant content of either 15-homoamberene (III) or 1-methylamberene (X) (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Kawamura et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of certain compounds in the GC-MS analysis and provides figures.

claim: A total of 166 bioinclusions were obtained out of 918 g of aerial amber.
source: A total of 166 bioinclusions were obtained out of 918 g of aerial amber (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2); about one third of them are well to exceptionally well preserved.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of bioinclusions found in a specific amount of amber.

claim: About one third of the bioinclusions are well to exceptionally well preserved.
source: A total of 166 bioinclusions were obtained out of 918 g of aerial amber (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2); about one third of them are well to exceptionally well preserved.
evidence: The manuscript describes the preservation quality of the bioinclusions.

claim: Plant inclusions are present, such as numerous fern or conifer trichomes and other undetermined remains.
source: Plant inclusions are present, such as numerous fern or conifer trichomes (not considered in the inclusion count) and other undetermined remains (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-E).
evidence: The manuscript describes plant inclusions found in the amber and provides figures.

claim: The diverse assemblage is chiefly composed of arthropods or remains of their activity, such as spiderweb threads and coprolites, but also a few vertebrate integumentary remains.
source: The diverse assemblage is chiefly composed of arthropods or remains of their activity, such as spiderweb threads (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F,G) and coprolites, but also a few vertebrate integumentary remains.
evidence: The manuscript describes the composition of the bioinclusion assemblage and provides figures.

claim: Arthropods are represented by arachnids and 11 insect orders.
source: Arthropods are represented by arachnids and 11 insect orders.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the arthropod diversity found in the amber.

claim: Arachnid inclusions belong to mites (Acari) and spiders (Araneae).
source: Arachnid inclusions belong to mites (Acari) and spiders (Araneae).
evidence: The manuscript identifies the arachnid groups found in the amber.

claim: Mites include a rare trombidiform of the family Rhagidiidae, an oribatid, and an undetermined six-legged larva.
source: Mites include a rare trombidiform of the family Rhagidiidae, an oribatid, and an undetermined six-legged larva (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript identifies specific mite taxa found in the amber and provides a figure.

claim: Five amber pieces with arthropods as syninclusions have spiderwebs preserved.
source: Five amber pieces with arthropods as syninclusions have spiderwebs preserved; although all are isolated strands, one tangled sample might correspond to a partial web (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The manuscript describes spiderweb inclusions found in the amber and provides a figure.

claim: Glue droplets on several strands suggest one spiderweb belonged to an orb web.
source: In the latter, glue droplets on several strands suggest it belonged to an orb web (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The manuscript infers the type of spiderweb based on observed features and provides a figure.

claim: The insect orders found in the Ariño amber are jumping bristletails (Archaeognatha), crickets (Orthoptera), cockroaches (Blattodea), barklice (Psocodea), thrips (Thysanoptera), whiteflies and aphids (Hemiptera), lacewings (Neuroptera), beetles (Coleoptera), moths (Lepidoptera), gnats, midges, and other flies (Diptera), and wasps (Hymenoptera).
source: The insect orders found in the Ariño amber are jumping bristletails (Archaeognatha), crickets (Orthoptera), cockroaches (Blattodea), barklice (Psocodea), thrips (Thysanoptera), whiteflies and aphids (Hemiptera), lacewings (Neuroptera), beetles (Coleoptera), moths (Lepidoptera), gnats, midges, and other flies (Diptera), and wasps (Hymenoptera).
evidence: The manuscript lists the insect orders identified in the amber.

claim: Archaeognaths are represented by the inclusion of a cercus and a medial caudal filament.
source: Archaeognaths are represented by the inclusion of a cercus and a medial caudal filament.
evidence: The manuscript describes the archaeognath remains found in the amber.

claim: Two orthopterans are poorly preserved, but one could belong to †Elcanidae.
source: Two orthopterans are poorly preserved, but one could belong to †Elcanidae.
evidence: The manuscript describes the orthopteran inclusions and provides a tentative identification.

claim: A blattodean nymph and an adult have been found, as well as several remains such as probably blattodean isolated antennae.
source: A blattodean nymph and an adult have been found, as well as several remains such as probably blattodean isolated antennae.
evidence: The manuscript describes the blattodean inclusions found in the amber.

claim: Among the seven psocodeans discovered, new taxa probably within the †Archaeatropidae and Manicapsocidae have been recognised.
source: Among the seven psocodeans discovered, new taxa probably within the †Archaeatropidae and Manicapsocidae have been recognised.
evidence: The manuscript describes the psocodean inclusions and indicates the presence of new taxa.

claim: Thysanopterans are the third most abundant insect order in the Ariño amber, with 11 specimens.
source: Thysanopterans are the third most abundant insect order in the Ariño amber, with 11 specimens (Figure 4B and C); three amber pieces contain more than one thrips as syninclusions.
evidence: The manuscript reports the abundance of thysanopterans in the amber and provides figures.

claim: Three amber pieces contain more than one thrips as syninclusions.
source: Thysanopterans are the third most abundant insect order in the Ariño amber, with 11 specimens (Figure 4B and C); three amber pieces contain more than one thrips as syninclusions.
evidence: The manuscript describes the occurrence of multiple thrips in single amber pieces.

claim: One isolated thrips shows a thin milky coating.
source: One isolated thrips shows a thin milky coating (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I), also found in other inclusions, and an infrequent nymph is unusually well preserved (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript describes a taphonomic feature observed on a thrips inclusion and provides a figure.

claim: An infrequent thrips nymph is unusually well preserved.
source: One isolated thrips shows a thin milky coating (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I), also found in other inclusions, and an infrequent nymph is unusually well preserved (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the preservation quality of a thrips nymph and provides a figure.

claim: Hemipterans comprise four representatives of Sternorrhyncha and two incomplete undetermined specimens.
source: Hemipterans comprise four representatives of Sternorrhyncha and two incomplete undetermined specimens.
evidence: The manuscript describes the hemipteran inclusions found in the amber.

claim: Three hemipterans have been identified as Aleyrodidae, probably belonging to the Aleurodicinae.
source: Three of the former have been identified as Aleyrodidae, probably belonging to the Aleurodicinae (Figure 4D), and are preserved in the same amber piece as syninclusions.
evidence: The manuscript identifies specific hemipteran taxa and provides a figure.

claim: The three aleyrodid hemipterans are preserved in the same amber piece as syninclusions.
source: Three of the former have been identified as Aleyrodidae, probably belonging to the Aleurodicinae (Figure 4D), and are preserved in the same amber piece as syninclusions.
evidence: The manuscript describes the occurrence of multiple aleyrodids in a single amber piece.

claim: An Aphidoidea specimen has been found in an amber piece with spiderweb strands.
source: In addition, an Aphidoidea specimen (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) has been found in an amber piece with spiderweb strands.
evidence: The manuscript describes an aphidoid inclusion and its association with spiderweb, and provides a figure.

claim: The neuropteran record consists of two wing impressions on amber surfaces probably belonging to Berothidae and a complete specimen, which could correspond to a †Paradoxosisyrinae (Sisyridae).
source: The neuropteran record consists of two wing impressions on amber surfaces probably belonging to Berothidae (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) and a complete specimen, which could correspond to a †Paradoxosisyrinae (Sisyridae) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the neuropteran inclusions and provides tentative identifications, with figures.

claim: Five coleopteran specimens have been discovered, two tentatively identified as belonging to Ptinidae and Cantharidae.
source: Five coleopteran specimens have been discovered, two tentatively identified as belonging to Ptinidae (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D) and Cantharidae (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The manuscript describes the coleopteran inclusions and provides tentative identifications, with figures.

claim: A ditrysian lepidopteran larva, yet incomplete anteriorly, is remarkably well preserved.
source: A ditrysian lepidopteran larva, yet incomplete anteriorly, is remarkably well preserved (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript describes a lepidopteran larva inclusion and its preservation quality, and provides a figure.

claim: Dipterans are represented by 19 specimens of the families †Archizelmiridae, Cecidomyiidae, Ceratopogonidae (including at least one female), Chironomidae, Mycetophilidae, Rhagionidae, Scatopsidae, and probably Psychodidae.
source: Dipterans (Figure 4F) are represented by 19 specimens of the families †Archizelmiridae, Cecidomyiidae, Ceratopogonidae (including at least one female), Chironomidae, Mycetophilidae, Rhagionidae, Scatopsidae, and probably Psychodidae.
evidence: The manuscript describes the dipteran inclusions and identifies families, and provides a figure.

claim: The †Archizelmiridae dipteran is represented by a well-preserved male within the genus Burmazelmira.
source: The first group is represented by a well-preserved male within the genus Burmazelmira (Figure 4F).
evidence: The manuscript identifies a specific dipteran genus and provides a figure.

claim: Hymenopterans are the most abundant insects in Ariño amber, accounting for 34 specimens belonging to the Platygastroidea, Mymarommatoidea, †Serphitidae, and †Stigmaphronidae.
source: Lastly, hymenopterans are the most abundant insects in Ariño amber, accounting for 34 specimens belonging to the Platygastroidea, Mymarommatoidea, †Serphitidae, and †Stigmaphronidae (Figure 4G‒I).
evidence: The manuscript reports the abundance and diversity of hymenopterans in the amber and provides figures.

claim: A new vertebrate inclusion is represented by a basal feather barb portion with a pennaceous structure.
source: Furthermore, a new vertebrate inclusion is represented by a basal feather barb portion with a pennaceous structure (Figure 4J).
evidence: The manuscript describes a feather inclusion found in the amber and provides a figure.

claim: Charophytes sampled from the level AR-1 comprise four species belonging to the families †Clavatoraceae and Characeae.
source: Charophytes sampled from the level AR-1 comprise four species belonging to the families †Clavatoraceae and Characeae.
evidence: The manuscript reports the charophyte diversity found in AR-1.

claim: The charophyte assemblage is dominated by †Clavatoraceae, particularly by well-preserved fructifications of Atopochara trivolvis var. trivolvis and Clavator harrisii var. harrisii (n > 100 for each species).

source: Overall, fern spores such as Appendicisporites spp. (Figure 5N), Cicatricosisporites spp., Cyathidites australis, Cyathidites minor (Figure 5O), and Gleicheniidites senonicus, predominate (13.48–38.42%) over those of bryophytes and lycophytes (1.44–2.38%).

source: Gymnosperms are namely represented by Inaperturopollenites dubius (12.79–20.36%) (Figure 5P), related to taxodioid conifers (Stuchlik et al., 2002), and the genus Classopollis (9.39–15.95%) (Figure 5Q), produced by †Cheirolepidiaceae conifers (Taylor and Alvin, 1984).

source: The Limnocytheridae are represented by Theriosynoecum cf. fittoni (Figure 5U and V) (n = 20) and Rosacythere denticulata (n > 70) (Figure 5W–BB).
evidence: The manuscript reports the abundance of limnocytherid ostracods and provides figures.

claim: Three variants of Rosacythere denticulata have been detected: one with a faint pitting and extremely small rosette ornamentation, one with a well-developed rosette, and one with strongly developed rosette and spine-like nodes.
source: Although the latter species was previously identified in Ariño (Tibert et al., 2013), three variants have now been detected: one with a faint pitting and extremely small rosette ornamentation (Figure 5W), one with a well-developed rosette (Figure 5X, Y and AA, Figure 5—figure supplement 1Q–U), and one with strongly developed rosette and spine-like nodes locally generated at the postero-dorsal and postero-ventral parts of the carapace (Figure 5Z and BB, Figure 5—figure supplement 1V–Y).
evidence: The manuscript describes new variants of Rosacythere denticulata and provides figures.

claim: †Cyprideidae and Cyprididae are found for the first time in Ariño, represented by the species Cypridea cf. clavata (n = 35) and Mantelliana sp. (n = 12), respectively.
source: †Cyprideidae and Cyprididae are found for the first time in Ariño, represented by the species Cypridea cf. clavata (n = 35) (Figure 5CC and DD) and Mantelliana sp. (n = 12) (Figure 5EE), respectively.
evidence: The manuscript reports the first occurrence of these ostracod families in Ariño and provides figures.

claim: The kidney-shaped, bioinclusion-lacking amber pieces from AR-1's lower amber-bearing layer were produced by roots.
source: The kidney-shaped, bioinclusion-lacking amber pieces from AR-1's lower amber-bearing layer were produced by roots.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the origin of the kidney-shaped amber based on their characteristics and stratigraphic context.

claim: Subterranean accumulations from both Recent/subfossil resin in modern forests and amber in geological deposits have been partly attributed to roots.
source: Subterranean accumulations from both Recent/subfossil resin in modern forests and amber in geological deposits have been partly attributed to roots (Langenheim, 1967; Langenheim, 2003; Henwood, 1993; Martínez-Delclòs et al., 2004; Seyfullah et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on subterranean resin accumulations.

claim: The resiniferous capacity of roots is well known.
source: Although the resiniferous capacity of roots is well known (Langenheim, 2003), observations of resin attached and/or associated with roots from both angiosperms and gymnosperms have been occasional (Langenheim, 1967; Seyfullah et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on the resiniferous capacity of roots.

claim: Field observations of late Pleistocene copal pieces produced and still attached to roots, covered by original soil, in an Agathis australis overturned stump show similar morphologies to the Ariño kidney-shaped amber pieces.
source: Our field observations of late Pleistocene copal pieces produced and still attached to roots, covered by original soil, in an Agathis australis overturned stump, which was formerly referred to but not figured (Najarro et al., 2009; Speranza et al., 2015), show similar morphologies to the Ariño kidney-shaped amber pieces (Figure 2J and K).
evidence: The manuscript describes field observations of modern copal for comparison with Ariño amber and provides figures.

claim: The Ariño's lower amber layer is interpreted as a root layer where the abundant and complete amber pieces are strictly in situ.
source: The Ariño's lower amber layer is interpreted as a root layer where the abundant and complete amber pieces are strictly in situ, that is, they are located exactly where the roots of the resiniferous trees exuded this resin in the subsoil (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript interprets the taphonomy of the lower amber layer based on field observations and provides a figure.

claim: This is the first time strictly in situ amber is reported.
source: This is the first time strictly in situ amber is reported; the scarcely fossiliferous, autochthonous-parautochthonous Triassic amber droplets from the Dolomites are preserved in a palaeosol (Schmidt et al., 2012; Seyfullah et al., 2018), but they are strictly ex situ, as the resin at least fell by gravity from their above-ground exudation location to the forest floor (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript claims novelty for the strictly in situ amber and compares it to other amber deposits, citing references.

claim: The fragile surface protrusions and microprotrusions of the kidney-shaped amber pieces from the lower layer would not have preserved even if minimal biostratinomic transport or other processes entailing abrasion had occurred.
source: Also, the fragile surface protrusions and microprotrusions of the kidney-shaped amber pieces from this layer would not have preserved even if minimal biostratinomic transport or other processes entailing abrasion had occurred (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: The manuscript infers the lack of transport based on the preservation of delicate surface features and provides figures.

source: Although other amber-bearing outcrops from the Iberian Peninsula have commonly yielded kidney-shaped amber pieces (Alonso et al., 2000; Peñalver et al., 2007; Najarro et al., 2009), these appear fragmented and in pockets together with aerial amber and generally have smoother surfaces and more regular morphologies than those from Ariño.
evidence: The manuscript compares the Ariño kidney-shaped amber to those from other localities, citing references.

source: Although these microscopic inclusions likely correspond to fossilised sap-resin emulsions (Lozano et al., 2020), at least partially, they show more complex and previously undocumented morphologies and arrangements.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the nature of the microscopic inclusions based on their characteristics and cites a reference.

source: Moreover, pyrite cuboctahedrons (Figure 2H) are usually found as mineralisations in the alleged empty spaces left by fluid bubble-like inclusions within amber (Alonso et al., 2000); they have been related to early diagenesis in reducing environments produced by anaerobic bacteria (Allison, 1990).

evidence: The manuscript claims novelty for the iron sulphate minerals in amber.

source: In contrast, the iron sulphate minerals growing in these spaces (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A) have not been previously reported; they could have formed during late diagenesis under oxidising conditions after the input of oxygenated water into the amber (Allison, 1990).

source: Indeed, the three previously reported localities where fossiliferous amber was found associated with dinosaur bonebeds, all from the Late Cretaceous, show clear signs of being either allochthonous or clearly mixed assemblages in which at least a substantial part of the vertebrate remains suffered significant transport prior to burial (Néraudeau et al., 2003; Currie et al., 2008; DePalma, 2010):
